For internal degloving, I'm reasoning that this is a closed Morel-Lavallée type injury—shearing separation of skin from fascia without an open tear, so it doesn't qualify as a laceration or fit the traumatic wound category; none of the options seem to apply. Moving to internal derangement, I'm considering this as a mechanical joint disorder, like in the knee or TMJ, and checking whether it maps to a general disorder classification.

For internal fixation removal, I'm weighing whether this counts as a surgical treatment process versus an excision—since removing hardware isn't the same as excising tissue, a surgical procedure classification fits better. Internal organ fits cleanly under anatomical structure in UBERON. Now for internal organ injury, I'm working through whether this necessarily constitutes a wound, since organ injuries can include contusions that aren't technically wounds or lacerations—this distinction matters for how it gets classified under the injury hierarchy.

For row 7, internal resection could map to either excision or surgical treatment process, but given it's a surgical removal procedure in a different branch than the one used for amputation, I'll keep consistency and go with excision.

Row 8: internal tissue should map to tissue as an anatomical structure, since tissue fits the definition of a collection of cell components not confined to one cell and is classified as an anatomical structure in UBERON.

Row 9 is trickier — "internal-organ repair" could refer either to a biological tissue repair process or a surgical repair procedure for injured organs, and the hyphenated phrasing suggests a surgical context like abdominal reconstruction, so I'm weighing whether to lean biological or surgical here.

Rows 10-14 all look like wound classification systems and scales (NPUAP-EPUAP, international systems, ISTAP and its grades) that fit cleanly under their assigned categories, so those stand. Row 15's IPN fits as a polymer network material, and I'm now considering row 16's IPN hydrogel as a polymer-water mixture.

Moving to interprofessional wound care — that's mostly a treatment process, so it stands. For the interrupted 3-0 non-absorbable suture, I'm weighing whether this refers to the stitch placement style (interrupted) or just classifies as a thread material, since it's a suture in situ made of non-absorbable thread.

I'll go with suture in situ [3] as the safer classification over simple interrupted [1], since "interrupted" could also cover mattress variants. Interrupted closure as a wound closure process using interrupted sutures stands at [3]. Interrupted figure-of-eight is actually a suture technique rather than a shape, so that classification doesn't apply — none.

Looking at the first row on immune cell chemotaxis, I'm tracing the GO hierarchy — chemotaxis falls under taxis/locomotion and cell motility, which rolls up to cellular process, so that classification holds up.

For immune cell cluster, I'm thinking this fits anatomical group since it describes component structures in close proximity, so that stands too.

Immune cell compartment seems more like a cellular component concept rather than anything else, so I don't think there's a good match here — marking it none.

Immune cell density seems like a composition quality, related to cellularity or quantity of subparts, so that one holds.

Immune cell homing doesn't consistently tie to wounding response since it covers things like lymphocyte homing to lymph nodes, so I'm leaning toward no match for this one either.

Now I'm moving to immune cell phenotype, which seems to reference things like M1/M2 macrophage polarization states in the context of wound healing.

Actually, subset naming is about the grouping itself rather than individual cells, so I'll leave it as none.

Row 10: Immune change is too vague to imply inflammation specifically, so none.

Row 11: Immune checkpoint molecule — proteins like PD-1 are molecular entities; while they're technically heteroatomic or p-block entities, the more meaningful classification is as a protein/macromolecule, so I'll stick with molecular entity as the most sensible fit.

Row 12: Immune clearance mostly maps to defense response, even though clearance of debris isn't strictly defensive — it's a reasonable fit, so it stands.

Row 13: Immune complex-mediated vasculitis fits under angiopathy given the vessel wall inflammation, likely more specifically a small-vessel/microangiopathy since it's typically leukocytoclastic vasculitis.

Row 14: Immune disorder doesn't map cleanly to a disorder-development process, so I'll leave it as none.

Row 15: Immune function is a physiological function rather than a role, so biological role and clinical function don't quite fit — I'm leaning toward none here too.

Row 16: Immune homeostasis maps well to GO's homeostatic process under biological regulation — that one stands.

Row 17: Immune imbalance fits as an abnormality of the immune system per HPO.

Row 18: Immune marker is trickier since markers can be cells, cytokines, or CD proteins rather than strictly informational biomacromolecules — I'll mark this as none since it doesn't consistently fit one category.

Row 19: Immune mediator includes small molecules like histamine, prostaglandins, and NO, not just biomacromolecules, so I should switch this to molecule instead.

Row 20: Immune microenvironment represents surrounding cells and molecules rather than a spatial region itself, so this one gets none.

For row two, distal extremity perfusion is a vascular process, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's a type of blood circulation or belongs under a broader vascular process category in GO.

Row 3's distal femoral shaft fracture doesn't hold up as a wound type since closed fractures aren't wounds, so I'm marking that one for removal. Row 4's distal foot amputation could reasonably fit under excision despite OBI's definition being lab-oriented, so I'm leaning toward keeping that relationship. Row 5 involves a gut-organ axis, which seems like more of a conceptual system than a physical entity.

Rows 6-9 run through similar issues: distal humeral fracture gets the same treatment as the femoral case and gets dropped, distal incision is tricky since surgical wounds are material entities rather than immaterial ones so I'm leaning toward excluding it, distal injury is too broad a category to map cleanly onto wound subtypes so that's out too, and distal insertion raises questions about whether UBERON's muscle insertion concept counts as a material anatomical structure.

I'll lean toward stands for muscle insertion as an attachment site.

For distal lesion, lesion doesn't fit the anatomical cluster category, and no broader wound term is offered, so none. Distal lower extremity fits as a gross anatomical part, so stands. Distal lower extremity wound isn't necessarily venous, and no generic wound term is available among the options, so none.

Distal medial gastrocnemius injury is typed as a process rather than fitting pressure impact, so none. Pseudoaneurysm isn't occlusive disease, so none. Distal mucous fistula is tricky — it's really a surgically created bowel stoma rather than a pathological disorder, so despite "fistula" suggesting pathology, I lean toward none since a wrong parent classification would be worse here.

For myotendinous junction, I'm reconsidering — this is specialized tissue, so it fits better as anatomical entity, changing to that parent.

Distal occlusive disorder is ambiguous between arterial and venous causes; angiopathy seems like the safer, more defensible parent since it broadly covers abnormal vessel lumen reduction, even though peripheral arterial occlusive disease is the likely specific context.

Row 18, distal pedal vein valve disruption — this seems more like a causative structural event leading to venous insufficiency rather than a disease type itself, so I'll leave it as none. Rows 19 and 20, distal phalanx and distal posterior cortex, both fit cleanly as gross anatomical parts, so they stand as is.

For EGCG, the C-O bonds classify it as an organochalcogen compound, which fits under heteroorganic entity and chalcogen molecular entity in the classification hierarchy. Moving on to the next row to check.

Epigastric bruising — I'm weighing whether a bruise counts as a hematoma. A bruise is diffuse extravasated blood (ecchymosis) while a hematoma is a localized collection, so they're not strictly equivalent. Since offering a wrong parent is worse than none, I'll leave this one unclassified.

For epigenetic aging, GO classifies aging as a developmental process, and since epigenetic aging reflects changes captured by the epigenetic clock, it reasonably falls under that same developmental process category.

For epigenetic and metabolic reprogramming, I'm treating this as a form of biological regulation since it involves changes to gene expression and metabolic pathway activity — that classification seems to hold.

Epigenetic change fits as a cellular process without issue.

Epigenetic dysregulation was tagged as a material entity by the extractor, but dysregulation describes a process abnormality rather than a physical thing, so I'd leave this one unclassified too.

Epigenetic factor is trickier — it could refer to proteins, enzymes, or environmental influences like diet or stress, and in this context likely points to mechanisms such as DNA methylation.

Since environmental epigenetic factors aren't really molecules themselves, and mislabeling carries more risk than leaving it unclassified, I'm going with none here.

For epigenetic modification, I'm weighing whether this counts as biological regulation versus chromatin organization under cellular process — histone modification in GO terms falls under protein modification or chromatin organization rather than regulation directly, even though it often functions to regulate gene expression.

Row 10 through 13 continue similarly — epigenetic regulator covers proteins and noncoding RNAs under molecular entity, reprogramming and trained immunity fit biological regulation, and epigenomic response fits response to stimulus, so all stand. Row 14, episiotomy, is a surgical incision, and I'm checking whether excision terminology applies since incision doesn't quite fit removal of substance.

Row 15's episiotomy repair stands as a wound closure process. Row 16, episode of wounding, holds as a wound-causing process, while row 17, cellulitis episodes, has me weighing whether this skin infection counts as a disease process or fits under inflammatory response, since it's more of a disease course than a direct wound outcome.

Rows 18-19 on epithelial barrier and barrier function don't fit since epidermis isn't mucosa and function differs from closure quality, so both get removed. Row 20, epithelial cell, stands as is.

Looking at the first row, I'm weighing whether disorder progression fits as a course of disease process — progression seems like a worsening phase downstream of disorder development, distinct from perpetuation, so it's likely a part of the broader disease course rather than identical to it.

For the second row, disorder recurrence seems trickier since it involves a return after remission rather than ongoing perpetuation. I'm leaning toward treating recurrence as a new instance of disorder development, since the disorder essentially reappears and redevelops.

For the disorder stage question, I'm weighing whether "disease classification stage" matches it as a categorical value specification, versus matching the ICE classification result output instead. A stage label like "Stage 3" feels more like a value within a classification system, so I'm inclined toward the stage-as-value interpretation rather than overreaching into the output category.

Moving through more rows: shift-related disorders don't fit treatment process so I'm marking none, postoperative wound healing disorders stand as is_a wound healing disorder, and bone metabolism disorders don't have a good course-of-disease match so those get none too. Disorders of consciousness seem reasonable as pathological disorders, so I'll let that stand. Disorganized collagen synthesis is trickier since it's not strictly tied to impaired wound healing in every case.

Continuing through similar edge cases — disorganized extracellular matrix, displaced femoral-neck fracture, disposable wound ruler, and biofilm disruption — none of these cleanly map to the available parent categories like wound healing disorder, wound dressing, or debridement, so I'm marking them all none since the relationships aren't universally true.

For disrupted cell structure, I let it stand since disrupted structure fits as a morphology quality. Disrupted colony biofilm doesn't count since lab-grown colony biofilm on a membrane isn't the same as a wound biofilm, so that's none. Disrupted iron homeostasis is trickier — it's more of a process abnormality than a simple PATO quality, so I'm weighing whether "deviation from normal" fits or if a phenotypic abnormality classification would be more accurate.

For disrupted keratinocyte differentiation, I'm marking none since it's not specifically tied to wound healing. Disrupted tissue regeneration is harder to decide — by analogy to how impaired wound healing still counts as a kind of wound healing, disrupted tissue regeneration could arguably still count as tissue regeneration occurring abnormally, so I'm leaning toward keeping consistency with that pattern rather than defaulting to none.

Row 18's disrupted wound healing process stands as a match. Row 19 mirrors row 12, so it's none. Row 20's disruption of blood supply reads as a pathological event like trauma severing vessels rather than a defined GO physiological process, so that's none too.

Healing characteristic is trickier—I'm weighing whether it refers to a physical quality of the healing process itself or more to wound/scar appearance, and given the ambiguity I lean toward marking it none rather than risk a wrong parent. Since healing disorder is categorized as a disposition, I'm weighing whether it fits the disease definition—a disposition toward pathological processes—but this feels uncertain and risky to commit to, so I'll mark it as none rather than guess wrong.

I'll reconsider and classify Healing edge as is_a Anatomical entity [3], since that category covers both material and immaterial structures and the wound margin tissue fits safely there. Healing effect stays as a therapeutic function, since it describes an agent's capacity to promote healing rather than the outcome itself. Now I'm moving to Healing event, which seems to represent a discrete occurrence within the broader healing process.

For Healing event, I'm thinking it's better classified under Wound healing related physiological process [2] rather than as a kind of wound healing itself, since parts or stages of a process aren't necessarily subtypes of it. Healing evolution and Healing failure both seem fine as they stand—evolution tracks the course of healing over time, and failure aligns with impaired wound healing.

For disposition-type terms like Healing impairment disposition and Healing index, neither fits well as a process category—these seem more like measurement or classification concepts, so I'm leaving them unclassified. Healing measure is ambiguous too: it could mean either a therapeutic intervention or an outcome measurement like time-to-healing, and since the category given is process, I suspect the extractor assumed intervention, but I'm not confident enough to assign a parent here.

Row 3 is about "infection" being a material entity with 766 abstracts, while the proposed classification as a biological_process seems like a category mismatch since infection in wound care contexts might refer to the state or the organisms involved rather than the process itself.

For row 4, infection agent and pathogen are essentially synonymous as organisms that cause infection, so that mapping stands.

Row 5 considers infection assessment as a diagnostic process evaluating wound characteristics, which holds given infection status is relevant to wound characteristics, though a broader wound diagnostic process option also seems plausible.

For row 8, I'm weighing whether infection control fits under wound treatment process, but since infection control also covers prevention measures like hygiene rather than just treating existing wounds, I'm leaning toward not classifying it there.

For row 9, I'm examining infection control practice and whether it belongs under postoperative wound control or as a completely executed planned process, leaning toward the latter since a practice is inherently a planned process.

Rows 10-13 look fine as is: infection control rate stands as an information content entity, infection depth as a quality, and infection development plus its pathway as disorder development processes. Now I'm looking at row 14, infection disorder being classified under infection itself.

Row 15, infection disposition, seems off though — classifying it as a material disease entity doesn't fit since disposition to become infected isn't necessarily a disease; none of the existing categories capture a pathogen's disposition to infect well.

Row 16: infection dynamic could map to disease course or totality, but it might also just mean population dynamics of the microbe — I'll leave it as is, that seems reasonable.

Row 17: infection episode shouldn't be restricted to wound infection specifically; it's more like a disease course, since an episode represents a bounded occurrence of the infection process.

Row 18: infection focus as a kind of infection raises the question of whether a localized site counts as the infection itself or just a part of it.

Row 19: infection inflammatory marker categorized as an information entity seems acceptable given the general nature of that category.

Row 20: infection injury under wound complication process doesn't quite fit—tissue damage caused by infection isn't necessarily a wound complication, so I'm considering whether a different classification like wound infection process applies better.

Rows 11 through 14 seem to be edge cases that don't quite fit the wound ontology — environmental bacterial adhesion is just a step within colonization rather than a distinct process, environmental contamination doesn't match wound microbial burden qualities, environmental factor isn't clearly a causal role, and enzymatic is simply an adjective, so none of these appear to map cleanly.

Moving on, enzymatic activity falls under catalytic activity (a function/process), not a physical quality, so it doesn't map either. Enzymatic cofactor though matches directly with cofactor's definition since cofactors are inherently tied to enzyme function, so that's a change. Enzymatic collagenase preparation fits under substances used for enzymatic wound debridement given the wound-care context, so that one stands. Enzymatic cross-linking reaction seems too broad and chemistry-focused rather than tissue-repair specific, so no match there.

Looking further, enzymatic debriding agent essentially is the same concept as a substance used for enzymatic wound debridement, so I'm marking that as a change to same.

In the context of wound care, though, fibrotic process essentially equates to scar formation, so I'll keep the is_a relationship standing. Moving to enhanced/continuous inflammation, I'm weighing whether it's better classified under inflammation process versus inflammatory response. Even though persistent inflammation is pathological in chronic wounds, it still fits as an inflammatory response by definition, so I'll leave that classification as is.

For enhanced angiogenesis, classifying it under angiogenesis seems straightforward and I'll keep it there.

For enhanced antibiofilm activity, I'm debating whether this counts as a therapeutic function versus something else like a disposition or role—since in wound dressing contexts it's typically therapeutic, I'll let that classification stand despite some ambiguity.

Now looking at enhanced barrier precautions, I recognize this actually refers to CDC infection control precautions used in nursing homes rather than anything related to wound edge protection.

Moving through the remaining rows: fluid absorption ability fits as a wound moisture absorbance function, so that stands. A formulation being classified as a mixture seems reasonable even though the term is vague—it could refer to a gel or dressing product, but chemically it's still a mixture of ingredients, so I'll let it stand. Enhanced inflammation as an inflammation process checks out fine. Now I'm considering intra-operative irrigation in the context of wound irrigation procedures.

Intraoperative irrigation clearly fits under wound irrigation as a process. But intraoperative measures more broadly—things like glove changes or antibiotic prophylaxis—aren't necessarily surgical treatment themselves, so I don't think that mapping holds. For neovascularization, angiogenesis feels too narrow since neovascularization also covers vasculogenesis from progenitor cells; I'm weighing whether blood vessel development or blood vessel morphogenesis would be a better, broader fit instead.

Since both angiogenesis and vasculogenesis are themselves classified as blood vessel morphogenesis, that's actually the more accurate and specific parent to use here, so I'm revising that mapping. Now I'm turning to the photothermal effect, which is trickier to classify since it's more of a process or disposition—essentially how something converts light into heat—rather than a straightforward quality.

I think it's reasonable to let it stand under the given quality classification even though it's imperfect, since the alternatives like optical quality don't fit well given this typically involves near-infrared light rather than visible light, and reclassifying it as a wrong parent would be worse than leaving it moderately justified as-is. Moving on, enhanced PRP correctly stands as a processed material entity since it's produced through centrifugation, and enhanced cell proliferation also checks out fine as currently categorized.

Continuing through the rows, enhanced tissue debridement and regeneration both check out as correctly classified under their respective processes. For enhanced treatment, since the term could refer to treatment of various conditions beyond just wounds in the abstract, I think the safer, more generic classification as a disease/disorder treatment process fits better than assuming wound treatment specifically. Wound healing and enhancement of healing both look correctly tied to their healing process parents.

I'll let that stand since positive regulation of healing relates. For enhancing lymphatic drainage, I'm debating whether it counts as regulation of body fluid levels versus just being a therapeutic intervention like manual lymphatic drainage or compression — since it's more an intervention aim than a biological regulation process, I'll go with none.

Donor-site drain classification as a wound/soft tissue drain stands as appropriate. Donor-site fluid accumulation (seroma) raises the question of whether a wound pocket, which is more of a space or cavity, is the right fit here.

I'm now looking at "diseased lower extremity" and concluding that a limb bearing a disease isn't itself a disorder, so no match applies. For "disfiguring" as a quality, I'm weighing whether it counts as a morphology quality since it reflects abnormal shape or structure.

Moving to "disfiguring scar," I don't think all disfiguring scars are hypertrophic or constitute wound healing disorders, so I'm settling on no match there either, and I'm starting to examine "disfiguring surgical debridement" next.

Row 17, "dishwater fluid," is a thin grayish foul-smelling exudate classically seen in necrotizing fasciitis, so it stands as wound exudate. Row 20, "disorder flare," seems mismatched with the treatment process classification since a flare is part of a disease's natural course rather than a treatment step.

I'm weighing whether to go with "none" or "stands" for this fibrin/slough area concept, since sphacel is technically necrotic slough tissue distinct from fibrin, but in practice wound scoring often lumps them together as yellow tissue coverage — I'll settle on stands since it's close enough to the fibrin coverage extent concept. For fibrinogen chain, that's clearly a polypeptide chain (alpha, beta, gamma), so that stands easily. Now I'm considering fibrinolysis, which is the breakdown of fibrin — it's a general hemostasis process rather than something specific to wound healing, so I need to decide whether it should be classified under wound healing or kept separate.

Not all fibrinolytic agents are enzymes — streptokinase itself lacks catalytic activity, it just activates plasminogen indirectly, so classifying this group under enzyme would be wrong. I'll leave it as none.
